extracted.intended_audience: statesmen, legislators, and politically engaged public (British/European context)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria for prudent legislation and political reform emphasizing respect for property, gradual improvement of institutions, and the moral qualities required of lawgivers. The guidance targets those designing or judging major institutional change (e.g., abolition/transfer of corporate property, revolutionary assemblies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for property and prescription
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules of prescription are part of the law of Nature; legislatures have no right to violate property, to overrule prescription, or to force a currency of their own fiction in place of that which is real.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that if prescription is shaken, no species of property is secure; legislative confiscation undermines the stability of property and injures all instruments that give property circulation. Anti-pattern: treating possession and prescription as nothing and authorizing confiscation as legitimate policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confiscation as a tool of public policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Confiscation and wholesale sale of established corporate or private property is unjust and dangerous; it tends to subvert all property and destroy established rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confiscation may begin with particular classes (bishops, monasteries) and then extend to princes and other proprietors; it produces unstable currency and arbitrary power. Policy justification must be evident and substantial to override the strong presumption against confiscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use existing institutional 'materials' rather than destroy them
rubrics_metrics.description: A good statesman should 'make the most of the existing materials' of his country (Spartam nactus es; hanc exorna) — preserve useful parts of old establishments and fit reforms to what is retained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than absolute destruction or unreformed existence, prefer preservation-plus-improvement. Anti-pattern: treating the country as 'carte blanche' and abolishing institutions wholesale without adapting their useful capacities for public benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve-and-improve as the standard of statesmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: The disposition to preserve coupled with the ability to improve should be the standard of a statesman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A competent politician balances conservation and improvement, using the enduring strengths of institutions while correcting defects. Those who only destroy or only conserve lack true statesmanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise of public power should be legitimate and conform to prescription
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorities that derive power outside settled law or necessity (e.g., revolutionary assemblies) lack the ordinary sanctions of constitutional legitimacy and thus invite critical scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revolutions require strong justification; powers assumed 'from no law and no necessity' are to be viewed skeptically. Anti-pattern: accepting the authority of an assembly simply because it seized power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid untried speculative schemes in public matters
rubrics_metrics.description: In matters of public interest the Assembly abandons decisions to 'untried speculations' and schemes that lack experience to prove benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-making should be grounded in experience and proven practice; relying on loose theories and experiments risks widespread harm. Anti-pattern: sweeping reforms justified solely by speculative benevolence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confront difficulty; value deliberation and skill over sloth
rubrics_metrics.description: True lawmakers must be willing to 'wrestle with difficulty' — they must have perseverance, resources of understanding, and not seek superficial quick fixes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid slothful solutions that elude difficulty through destruction; the capacity to face and resolve complex problems is essential. Anti-pattern: preferring easy abolition to hard constructive work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawgivers should be humane, sensible, and self-fearing
rubrics_metrics.description: The true lawgiver ought to have 'a heart full of sensibility' — to love and respect mankind and to 'fear himself' (be self-aware and cautious).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative movements should be deliberate and guided by sensibility to human consequences. Anti-pattern: unfeeling zeal or unbounded confidence in abstract designs without regard for human costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider moral and social effects of reallocating surplus
rubrics_metrics.description: When transferring landed capital (surplus product), a legislator must ensure the capital returns to industry with minimal moral detriment to those who spend it or to the people who receive it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the character and likely expenditures of current possessors with proposed purchasers (virtue, industry, sobriety, propensity to extort). Anti-pattern: assuming purchasers will better serve public ends without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the civic uses of seemingly 'superstitious' institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutions labelled superstitious (monasteries, religious corporations) may still provide durable public resources: revenues directed to public purposes, disciplined personnel, libraries, records, collections, and other cultural goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before abolishing such institutions, explore ways to correct abuses while preserving their beneficial public functions. Anti-pattern: destroying institutions wholesale because of some superstitious elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer public direction of corporate bodies to arbitrary private dispersion
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate bodies and their fortunes are particularly suited to long-term public uses and are more susceptible to public direction than scattered private holders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformers should consider directing corporate property for public ends rather than dispersing it through sale, which risks caprice and loss of enduring public benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware contagion of fanaticism and proselytism
rubrics_metrics.description: Epidemical fanaticism and widespread proselytism produce social confusion, destroy common feelings of nature, and incubate violence against property and order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against the spread of writings, sermons, and societies that incite hatred of established institutions; monitor transnational networks that propagate subversive doctrines. Anti-pattern: romanticizing or applauding fanatical movements as models for imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain fidelity to public credit and justice to avoid destabilizing parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive public debt and mismanagement that offends creditors risks producing powerful, discontented moneyed interests that may seek new energetic (and unjust) governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments should manage public debt prudently; failure either way (heavy impositions or default) can create dangers to civil order. Anti-pattern: allowing public finances to incentivize contempt for justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use power instruments wisely; do not sell public 'tools' through improvidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where institutions provide a 'power' for public benevolence (revenues, disciplined personnel), politicians should convert and harness those resources thoughtfully, not sell them off through improvident means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke criticizes selling the 'tools' (monastic revenues and men) because politicians 'do not understand their trade' and thus 'sell their tools.' Anti-pattern: treating institutional assets as immediate cash sources without planning for their public utility.
